questions.prompt: Say the same thing in fewer words: "a journey that lasts twenty days" is …
questions.explanation: A number and a noun welded by a hyphen make a compound adjective, and the noun inside it never takes -s: a twenty-day journey, exactly as we say a ten-minute talk or a 200-page book. Keeping "days" is the commonest mistake of all, because the journey really does last twenty days; dropping the hyphen leaves two loose words the reader has to join alone; and the apostrophe of "twenty-day's" would claim the journey belongs to the days.

questions.prompt: The last line of a leaflet reads: "Meet in the Education Centre foyer." Where do you wait?

options.text: the entrance hall of the building
the desk where tickets are sold
the room where drinks are served
the hall in which the show is given

questions.explanation: A foyer is the entrance hall, the large open space you step into just inside the doors — which is why leaflets use it as a meeting point: everybody passes through it. The desk where tickets are sold is the box office, the drinks themselves are the refreshments, and the hall where the show is given is the auditorium or the concert hall.

questions.prompt: A Friday leaflet prints four events. Holiday Fun · 10.00 am · Studio 2 · children 6–11 · £3. Guided Tour · 11.00 am · main foyer · £4. Interactive Talk · 2.30 pm · Room 10 · free, book in advance. Youth Arts Party · 7–9 pm · whole building · ages 12–19 · free, no need to book. Karim is 16, reaches the centre after six in the evening and has booked nothing. Which event can he attend?
questions.explanation: Three conditions have to be satisfied at once, and only the Youth Arts Party satisfies all three: it runs from 7 to 9 pm, so it is still on when he arrives; it is open to ages 12–19, and he is 16; and it says "no need to book", which he has not done. The two morning events are over long before he gets there, and the Interactive Talk fails twice — it began at half past two, and although it is free it still has to be booked in advance. Free and booked are two different conditions: free is about money, booking is about a seat.

questions.prompt: Which of these words carries its main stress on the SECOND syllable?
questions.explanation: Say them slowly and count: per-FOR-mance puts the stress on its second syllable. CIN-e-ma is stressed at its opening, on CIN. The other two both land on the third: ex-hi-BI-tion obeys the rule that -ion pulls the stress onto the syllable just before it, and in-ter-AC-tive follows the same movement. Stress is not decoration — put it in the wrong place and a listener may not recognise the word at all.

questions.prompt: A museum shop advertises "science-inspired gifts". What does that compound adjective tell you about them?

options.text: they make you want to study science
they were made by a scientist

questions.explanation: Unpack a noun + past participle compound by turning it round: science-inspired means inspired by science, so the idea and the design of the gift come from science. The direction matters — the gifts are inspired, they do not inspire, so "they make you want to study science" reverses the arrow. Being inspired by science does not mean being made by a scientist either, nor teaching anything: a science-inspired scarf may simply be printed with the shape of a molecule.
